terminal.description: A shell in your workspace where try.js hashes a password twice, checks a right and a wrong one, and prints what the staff store holds.

tasks.title: Hash a password with a salt
tasks.description:
Implement `hashPassword(password)` in `src/passwords.js`. It returns one string, `'<salt>:<hash>'`:

- the salt is 16 random bytes, new on every call, written as hex
- the hash is 64 bytes of scrypt of the password, with the salt's hex text as the salt, written as hex
- the password itself is nowhere in the result

The check hashes passwords of its own, each one twice, and works out the scrypt of each from the salt you returned.
nextSteps: Run `node try.js` and read what it prints today.
Make the salt and write it as hex.
Hash the password with that salt.
Join the two parts and run `node try.js` again.
hints: Everything you need is in `node:crypto`, and the lesson's part on salt shows each piece on its own.
`randomBytes(16)` gives the salt's bytes and `scryptSync(password, salt, 64)` the hash's. Both are Buffers, and a Buffer becomes hex text with `.toString('hex')`.
Make `const salt = randomBytes(16).toString('hex')` first, give that text to `scryptSync`, and return the two hex strings joined with a `:`.

videos.title: Why a site keeps a hash, not the password

tasks.title: Check a password against its hash
tasks.description:
Implement `verifyPassword(password, stored)` in `src/passwords.js`. `stored` is a value `hashPassword` made. It returns `true` when `password` is the one it was made from, and `false` otherwise:

- it compares the two hashes in constant time
- a stored value that is not a salt and a hash, or whose hash has another length, gives `false` and never throws

The check makes stored values of its own and tries the right password, near misses, plain text and broken values. It also watches how the hashes are compared.
nextSteps: Split the stored value into its salt and its hash.
Hash the typed password the same way `hashPassword` did.
Compare the two in constant time.
Make a broken stored value answer `false`, then run `node try.js`.
hints: A hash cannot be turned back into a password. To check one, you make a second hash the same way and see whether the two match.
The salt comes from the stored value, not from new random bytes. `timingSafeEqual(a, b)` compares two Buffers of the same length and throws when their lengths differ.

`const [salt, hash] = stored.split(':')`, then `Buffer.from(hash, 'hex')` and `scryptSync(password, salt, 64)`. Return `false` when a part is missing or the lengths differ, and `timingSafeEqual` of the two otherwise.

tasks.title: Save staff without their password
tasks.description:
Implement `addStaff(staff, person)` in `src/staff.js`. `person` is `{ name, email, role, password }` and `staff` is a store from `createStaffStore()`.

- save the person with the store's `add()`, with a `passwordHash` field made by `hashPassword()` in place of the password
- the store never holds the password itself
- return the saved member as `{ id, name, email, role }`, with the id the store gave it and without the hash

The check adds people of its own to a fresh store, then reads everything the store holds.
nextSteps: Take the password out of the person.
Save the rest with its hash.
Return the member without the hash, then run `node try.js`.
hints: Whatever you hand to `add()` is what the store keeps, so the password must not be in it.
Destructuring with a rest element takes one field out and keeps the others: `const { password, ...rest } = person`.
`staff.add({ ...rest, passwordHash: hashPassword(password) })` saves it. Take `passwordHash` out of what `add()` returns the same way before you return it.
